h6: Diffusion is a free, public, open-source dashboard run by one person. There is nothing to buy and nothing to subscribe to, so these terms are mostly a description of what the site is rather than a contract you are being held to.
p: Read it, quote it, disagree with it in public. No permission needed.
Do not attack the server or try to reach other readers' accounts. There is nothing in them, but still.
There is no password to keep confidential.
A real name and a real address are appreciated. Neither is checked.
This is one person's project, and it may change or stop:
Nothing here costs money, and no part of it is held back for a paid tier.
An account used to attack the site will be removed.
The economic data on this site belongs to the statistical agencies that publish it, not to Diffusion. Each source carries its own licence, and that licence is shown on every series page.
Cite and link the publisher. For anything that matters, take the numbers from them rather than from here.
The code is MIT licensed and on GitHub. Do what you like with it.
The written analysis is its author's. The page design is adapted from a commercial template under that template's own licence.
The institutional reports cited in the literature sections belong to their publishers. They are linked and quoted, never redistributed.
There is no subscription, no paid tier and no trial.
No card is asked for and no payment is processed anywhere on this site.
If that ever changes it will be said plainly and in advance, not by quietly editing this page.
Diffusion is provided as is, with no warranty.
Data is ingested from public sources automatically and can be wrong, stale or misattributed. Where a page knows its evidence is weak, it says so on the page.
Nothing here is investment, financial or policy advice. It is a reading of published statistics.

Nothing is being agreed to that costs you anything.

/legal/privacy-policy.title: Privacy Policy — Diffusion
/legal/privacy-policy.description: What Diffusion stores about a reader — a name and an email address, nothing else — and the terms of using the site.
h6: Diffusion is run by one person and holds two pieces of information about you: a name and an email address, typed into a sign-in form. This page says what happens to them. It is short because very little happens to them.
p: This is the complete list, not a summary of it:
The name and the email address you type into the sign-in form.
Nothing else. No analytics, no tracking pixels, no advertising identifiers, no third-party scripts.
No record of what you read, no device fingerprint, and no IP address log kept against your account.
Anything you choose to send by email, which is read by one person.
The address is used for exactly one thing, and here is the honest version of it:
To know roughly who the work reaches. That is the entire reason an account exists.
To reply, if you write in with a correction.
You will not be emailed otherwise. There is no mailing list, no newsletter and no product announcement.
The address is never verified, so it is a visitor record rather than a credential, and it protects nothing.
Nothing behind the sign-in is private — it is public statistics from public sources — so there is nothing here for an account to guard.
The row is stored in a Postgres database and read by nobody but the person who runs the site.
Nothing is sold, rented, traded or shared. Not in aggregate either.
Nothing is inferred, scored, enriched or joined against any other source.
Nobody. Named individually, so this cannot be read generously:
The database host stores the row, because it stores every row. There is no analytics provider, because there are no analytics.
A lawful order would be complied with. There would be very little to hand over.
Google Fonts serves two typefaces to your browser, which means Google sees that request. That is the only external service any page here loads, and it is told nothing about you.

No password is set, sent, hashed or stored by either sign-in route, so there is nothing here that could be stolen and replayed against another site. A session is a signed cookie rather than a stored token. What is held is a name and an unverified email address, and no system can promise perfect security of even that.
Wherever you are, and without having to cite a regulation:
Email and ask what is stored under your address, or ask for it to be deleted. It will be, and you will get a reply saying so.
There is no processing to restrict, and the portable version of your record is a name and an email address.
Signing out and not coming back also works.
Questions about any of this, or about what is stored under your address: contact@atmos.com

/.description: Artificial intelligence's measurable effect on the world economy, read through five lenses and built only from official statistics. Every number links back to the agency that published it.

The rules are the point. Everything else is implementation

p: Each question shows the claim being tested, how this page measures it, and where it fails.
FRED, the World Bank, DBnomics, SEC EDGAR, Epoch AI and nineteen others. Every series links back to its publisher with its licence stated.
Not just the answer. The mechanism being claimed, the measurement used, and the confound that would break it.
Every claim sits directly above the series it rests on. Follow it in either direction.
These series say not yet. But several studies measuring at a finer grain say otherwise, and the likeliest reconciliation is that this page is asking at the wrong resolution.

How the data is gathered, how the claims are made, and where both fall short.
Where does the data come from?

From twenty-four public sources — FRED, the World Bank, DBnomics, SEC EDGAR, Epoch AI, the US Federal Register and others. Nothing is redistributed: every series links back to its publisher with its licence stated, so you can take the data on the publisher's terms rather than trusting a chart here.
Ingestion runs nightly. The prose does not — numbers move on their own and sentences do not follow them, so every page shows the date a person last checked its writing against its data.
Is any of this written by AI?

No figure is. Every number is computed in SQL from a named source, and every claim is written by a person and dated. Where a takeaway from an outside report was read out of the document by a machine, the page says so and gives the page number so you can check it.

That credible sources reach opposite conclusions, and the disagreement is the finding. Three pages currently carry it. The alternative — picking whichever result is tidier — is the thing this site exists not to do.
Take it from the publisher, on their terms — each one's licence is shown on its series page. The code is MIT and the whole project is open source.

Country coverage. One country has real depth; most carry six annual World Bank series and nothing else. Policy is thin. Occupation-level employment, which is what several questions actually need, is largely missing. All of that is stated on the pages it affects rather than hidden.
If you are an economist and a comparison here is unsound, that is the most useful thing you could tell me.
